topic: Children recognise brand logos before they can read
angle: Food advertising causes immediate increases in calorie consumption and influences brand attitudes in children, with combined media sources having a stronger effect.
title: The Architecture of Appetite

hooks.text: Does your child know why they want that snack?
You think they are choosing, but the ads are choosing.
You are letting brands shape your child's appetite.
A screen glows in a dark living room.

reveal.headline: Knowing how advertising works does not protect children.
reveal.body: Understanding the tactics of marketing fails to shield children from its impact on their brand and product attitudes.

explain.headline: Combined media sources increase food consumption.
explain.body: When children see food ads on TV and play advergames, the influence on their food consumption is stronger than TV ads alone.

matters.headline: The environment shapes dietary habits.
matters.body: That may be why children develop specific food preferences and increased intake shortly after exposure to unhealthy marketing.

example.headline: A child sits in front of a screen.
example.body: They watch a cartoon and play a mobile game while snacks sit on the table nearby.

question.headline: What is shaping your child's preferences?

stat.label: mean difference in dietary intake during or shortly after exposure to ads

claims.text: Greater understanding of advertising did not protect against the impact of advertising on brand or product attitudes.
claims.quote: We found greater understanding did not protect against the impact of advertising on brand or product attitudes.

claims.text: Online ('advergame') advertising combined with TV advertising causes a stronger influence on children's food consumption than TV advertising alone.
claims.quote: CONCLUSION: Online ('advergame') advertising combined with TV advertising exerted a stronger influence on children's food consumption than TV advertising alone.

claims.text: In children exposed to unhealthy dietary marketing, dietary intake significantly increased by a mean difference [MD] = 30.4 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.9 to 57.9) during or shortly after exposure to advertisements.
claims.quote: Our meta-analysis showed that in children exposed to unhealthy dietary marketing, dietary intake significantly increased (mean difference [MD] = 30. 4 kcal, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2. 9 to 57. 9, and MD = 4. 8 g, 95%CI 0. 8 to 8. 8) during or shortly after exposure to advertisements.

claims.text: Children exposed to food advertising on TV (11 studies) and advergames (five studies) respectively consumed an average 60.0 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.1-116.9) and 53.2 kcal (95% CI, 31.5-74.9) more than children exposed to nonfood advertising.
claims.quote: Meta-analysis revealed that children exposed to food advertising on TV (11 studies) and advergames (five studies) respectively consumed an average 60. 0 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI], 3. 1-116. 9) and 53. 2 kcal (95% CI, 31. 5-74. 9) more than children exposed to nonfood advertising.

claims.text: Acute exposure to food advertising causes increased food intake among children and adults.
claims.quote: These findings suggest that acute exposure to food advertising increases food intake among children and adults and that the middle occipital gyrus is an implicated brain region among children.

verdict: The evidence consistently shows that exposure to unhealthy food marketing leads to increased dietary intake and influences preferences in children.
caveat: Many studies were at high risk of bias, and some research focuses on acute exposure rather than long-term real-world effects.
caption:
Marketing influences children's food preferences and intake.
Research shows that exposure to unhealthy food ads leads to increased dietary intake, though some studies were at high risk of bias and focused on acute exposure.
